title: Transit-Oriented Development — Core Overview (Edition 1)
description: Transit-oriented development concentrates housing, jobs, and services within walking distance of high-capacity transit stations, typically a five to ten minute walk. The approach pairs higher-density mixed-use zoning with reduced parking requirements near stations. This overview edition presents Transit-Oriented Development as a core transit concept for contemporary cities.

principles: Design for frequency, speed, and reliability
Integrate fares and transfers across modes
Connect land use to stations

real_examples.fact: Curitiba's 1966 master plan built the city around five structural transit corridors, and its bus rapid transit system, launched in 1974 as the world's first full BRT, carries about 2.3 million passengers per day.

spec.source_note: Core facts verified from public sources.

title: Bus Rapid Transit — Core Overview (Edition 1)
description: Bus rapid transit gives buses rail-like speed and capacity through dedicated lanes, off-board fare collection, and platform-level boarding. Curitiba introduced the first full BRT system in 1974 after planners abandoned a costly light-rail plan in favor of a trunk-and-feeder bus network on segregated median lanes. This overview edition presents Bus Rapid Transit as a core transit concept for contemporary cities.

principles: Design for frequency, speed, and reliability
Integrate fares and transfers across modes
Connect land use to stations

real_examples.fact: Bogota's TransMilenio BRT opened in 2000 and became one of the busiest bus corridors in the world.

spec.source_note: Core facts verified from public sources.

title: R-1 Single-Family Residential Zoning — Core Overview (Edition 1)
description: In New York City's zoning code, R1 districts permit detached single-family homes and community facilities, the lowest-density residential category. Higher numbers after the R indicate greater permitted density, from R1 detached houses up to R10 residential towers. This overview edition presents R-1 Single-Family Residential Zoning as a core zoning concept for contemporary cities.

principles: Separate incompatible uses while allowing compatible mixes
Keep rules predictable and legible for applicants
Tie intensity to infrastructure capacity
mechanisms: Set bulk controls for FAR, height, and setbacks

real_examples.fact: New York's Zoning Resolution defines R1-1 and R1-2 as single-family detached residence districts.

spec.source_note: Core facts verified from public sources.

description: C1 and C2 commercial overlay districts are mapped on local commercial streets inside residential neighborhoods to host neighborhood-oriented retail and services. Commercial districts run from C1 neighborhood retail up to C8 districts that allow gas stations and car repair. This overview edition presents C-1 Commercial Overlay Districts as a core zoning concept for contemporary cities.

principles: Separate incompatible uses while allowing compatible mixes
Keep rules predictable and legible for applicants
Tie intensity to infrastructure capacity
mechanisms: Set bulk controls for FAR, height, and setbacks

real_examples.fact: Commercial overlays are designated C1-1 through C1-5 and C2-1 through C2-5 on the New York zoning maps.

title: M-1 Light Manufacturing Districts — Core Overview (Edition 1)
description: M1 districts permit light manufacturing alongside many commercial uses, while community facilities are limited and new residential development is generally not allowed. Heavier industry sits in M2 and M3 districts, with M3 allowing heavy manufacturing. This overview edition presents M-1 Light Manufacturing Districts as a core zoning concept for contemporary cities.

Tie intensity to infrastructure capacity
mechanisms: Set bulk controls for FAR, height, and setbacks

Pairing residence and manufacturing districts lets cities keep jobs near homes without heavy-industry conflicts. This overview edition presents Mixed-Use Special Districts as a core zoning concept for contemporary cities.

title: Urban Growth Boundary — Core Overview (Edition 1)
description: An urban growth boundary draws a legal line around a metro area, concentrating development inside and preserving farmland and open space outside. Oregon's 1973 statewide planning law required every city to adopt one, with Portland's boundary the best-known example. This overview edition presents Urban Growth Boundary as a core land-use concept for contemporary cities.

principles: Grow inward before outward
Remediate before abandoning
Balance jobs and housing

real_examples.fact: Portland's urban growth boundary, established under Oregon's 1973 land-use law, is expanded only after the region demonstrates land need.

spec.source_note: Core facts verified from public sources.

title: Floor Area Ratio — Core Overview (Edition 1)
description: Floor area ratio caps building bulk by limiting total floor area to a multiple of lot area. Cities trade higher FAR for public benefits such as affordable housing or plazas through density bonuses. This overview edition presents Floor Area Ratio as a core zoning concept for contemporary cities.

Tie intensity to infrastructure capacity
mechanisms: Set bulk controls for FAR, height, and setbacks

real_examples.fact: FAR is the standard bulk control in zoning codes worldwide.

title: Inclusionary Zoning — Core Overview (Edition 1)
description: Inclusionary zoning requires or incentivizes developers to set aside a share of new units at below-market rents. Programs typically pair the mandate with density bonuses so projects remain financially viable. This overview edition presents Inclusionary Zoning as a core housing concept for contemporary cities.

principles: Add supply at many price points
Protect existing residents from displacement
Locate homes near jobs and transit

real_examples.fact: Hundreds of cities use inclusionary zoning to produce income-restricted homes.
